column1: # mapping_set_title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 to NIST AI RMF (nist_ai_100_1 component) Schema Mappings

# mapping_set_description: Schema-level mappings between the ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (AI Management System) LinkML schema and the NIST AI RMF umbrella schema, narrowed to the NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0 core framework) child schema. Mapping rows are identical to those in iso42001-to-nist-ai-100-1.sssom.tsv but framed from the umbrella RMF perspective; consumers integrating against the merged nist-ai-rmf schema should prefer this set.

column10: comment
Both are the root container for an organisation's AI governance programme; ISO 42001 is certifiable while NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance
Same concept: the engineered AI system that is the subject of governance and risk management
AIRisk is the ISO 42001 AI-specific risk; NIST AI 100-1 Risk is the parallel concept with likelihood/impact and explicit AI-context
AIRisk is also a narrower match for AiSpecificRisk which highlights AI-only risk drivers (data drift, model opacity, automation bias)
Risk-treatment plan operationalises the organisation's risk tolerance posture; related but not equivalent (treatment vs tolerance threshold)
The ISO 42001 risk-assessment process aligns most closely with the NIST RMF MAP and MEASURE Functions taken together
AI-system impact assessment captures the impacts modelled by NIST's Impact class (sign, severity, affected population)
Recorded harms in NIST AI RMF correspond to materialised AI incidents in ISO 42001
A concern report often anticipates or surfaces a harm to people, organisations or ecosystems
The organisation is one of the AI actors in NIST's lifecycle taxonomy
Roles in ISO 42001 group accountabilities that NIST organises as actor-task assignments
Interested parties (including end users, affected communities, third parties) are NIST AI actors
ISO 42001 Annex A controls and NIST RMF Subcategories both express granular, actionable expectations
Documented information artefacts include the kind of guidance NIST publishes per Subcategory in its Playbook
Both enumerations describe AI-system lifecycle stages; granularity and naming differ but coverage is parallel
ISO 42001 inception aligns with NIST plan-and-design stage
Design stage is captured in NIST's combined plan-and-design
Direct equivalent
ISO development stage corresponds to NIST build-and-use-model
Direct equivalent
Direct equivalent
Direct equivalent
Continuous validation is part of NIST's operate-and-monitor stage
Re-evaluation is folded into NIST operate-and-monitor
NIST AI 100-1 does not break out a dedicated decommissioning stage; related to end-of-life within operate-and-monitor
Both enumerations partition AI ecosystem actors; ISO uses producer/customer/partner roles, NIST uses lifecycle-task actors
The provider supplies the AI system; closest NIST actor-task is development
Producer designs and builds; aligns with AI design actor task
Customer aligns with NIST end-users actor category
Partner aligns with third-party entities
AI subjects are individuals or groups affected by the system's decisions
Relevant authority maps to NIST governance and oversight actor task

ISO 42001 AI objectives largely mirror NIST's seven trustworthiness characteristics (valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, privacy-enhanced, fair with harmful bias managed)
Safety is a direct NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Secure and resilient is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Privacy-enhanced is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Fair with harmful bias managed is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Accountable and transparent is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Explainable and interpretable is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Valid and reliable is a NIST trustworthiness characteristic
Accountability is paired with transparency in NIST's enumeration
Robustness falls within NIST's valid-and-reliable and secure-and-resilient characteristics
ISO/IEC 31000 risk-treatment options (modify, accept, avoid, share) align directly with NIST's risk-response enumeration
Modify (treat) the risk
Accept the residual risk
Avoid the activity that creates the risk
Share/transfer the risk (insurance, contracts, joint ventures)
Both enumerate categories of AI harm; ISO enumerates specific incident types while NIST partitions harms by impacted entity
Bias incidents predominantly cause harm to people
Societal-scale harm aligns with NIST harm-to-an-ecosystem
Privacy breaches harm the individuals whose data is exposed
Security breaches typically harm the operating organisation
Risk sources in ISO 42001 overlap with the measurement-challenge categories NIST identifies as drivers of AI-specific risk
Direct equivalent (opacity / inscrutability)
ML-specific risks include emergent behaviours that NIST flags as a measurement challenge
Lifecycle-stage risk source is identical to NIST's measurement challenge category
Both slots capture the deployment context and intended purpose of an AI system
Intended use(s) for the AI system
Foreseeable / potential misuse scenarios (both MAP-1 / 6.1.4 expectations)
Human-oversight specification corresponds to NIST's human-AI configuration consideration
AI-system lifecycle stage reference (slot names match)
System events that escalate to incidents/harms; NIST tracks harms directly
Identified risks attached to a system or assessment
Chosen treatment / response option
Both express the residual risk after treatment
